name: Ultrasonic (piezo) rhinoplasty

lead: Ultrasonic or piezo rhinoplasty uses instruments driven by piezoelectric vibration to cut and shape the nasal bones. The payoff people want is a refined, straighter or lower bridge, with more precise bone cuts than hand chisels and rasps.

The instruments vibrate at ultrasonic frequency and cut bone while sparing soft tissue. A 2023 review says they allow precise osteotomies under direct visual control after an open or extended closed approach, plus ostectomies and rhinosculpture, and that they preserve bone stability. A general reference dates the technique to 2004 and describes the devices as similar to those used in dental surgery. A registered trial compares piezo with endonasal osteotomy on postoperative healing.

paras: It is used as the bone-sculpting step within an otherwise standard rhinoplasty, and it is also used in dorsal preservation work. Swelling needs to settle before the final bridge shape shows.

The sources describe the technique rather than comparative harms, so frequency of complications versus traditional tools is not documented. It carries the general risks of rhinoplasty, including swelling, asymmetry and revision. It is performed by surgeons under anaesthesia.

angle.text: Piezo rhinoplasty reshapes the nasal bones precisely, with a straighter or lower bridge as the visible result once swelling settles. Ultrasonic tools cut bone while sparing soft tissue, so the bone work can be more controlled than with chisels and rasps. Descriptions of its advantages come mostly from surgeon reviews.

lead: Ultrasonic rhinoplasty is a way of performing the bone work of rhinoplasty using piezoelectric instruments designed for the purpose. A 2023 review of ultrasonic rhinoplasty and septoplasty states that the instruments allow precise osteotomies under direct visual control after an open or extended closed approach, as well as ostectomies and rhinosculpture, and that they preserve bone stability by not damaging support structures and avoiding unwanted fractures.[1]

A general rhinoplasty reference dates the introduction of ultrasonic rhinoplasty to 2004 and credits it to Massimo Robiony; it describes the devices as similar to those used in dental surgery and sparing of soft tissue.[2]
Published comparative evidence in the sources reviewed is limited to a registered trial comparing piezo and endonasal osteotomy.[3]

paras: The 2023 review frames the technique as applicable to dorsum preservation and to dorsum structural reconstruction, and says it gives control over nasal bone cuts.[1] The general reference adds that it requires a more extensive surgical approach than closed techniques.[2]

No completed comparative studies appear in the sources reviewed. A registered trial of 60 patients (status unknown, begun 2023) compares piezo and endonasal osteotomy methods on postoperative healing in septorhinoplasty.[3] A registered trial of photobiomodulation for swelling after rhinoplasty is recruiting and is not specific to piezo technique.[4]

timeline.event: Ultrasonic rhinoplasty introduced, according to Wikipedia, by Massimo Robiony.[2]
